specPoints.text: understand how restriction enzymes are used to cut DNA at specific sites and ligase enzymes are used to join pieces of DNA together
understand how plasmids and viruses can act as vectors, which take up pieces of DNA, and then insert this recombinant DNA into other cells

primer.text: Genetic modification is molecular carpentry: restriction enzymes saw DNA at chosen sequences, sticky ends align the join, ligase glues it, and plasmid or virus vectors carry the recombinant cargo into bacteria, yeast or human cells. This note details the cutting and the delivery.

lessons.title: Molecular Scissors and Sticky Ends
lessons.opening: Genetic modification begins with surgery on DNA. Restriction enzymes each recognise particular base sequences and cut there, leaving short single-stranded sticky ends; cutting a plasmid with the same enzyme gives complementary overhangs that pair, and DNA ligase seals the fragments into one molecule.
keyPoints: Genetic modification moves a chosen gene across into a different organism's DNA.
Different restriction enzymes target different DNA sequences, so specific enzymes cut out the wanted gene.
Cutting with restriction enzymes leaves sticky ends, short single-stranded sections that pair with complementary overhangs.
A bacterial plasmid cut by the same restriction enzyme presents matching sticky ends.
DNA ligase joins gene and plasmid into a single unbroken DNA molecule.

low.restatement: Scissors find the right word in the sentence, cut, and leave jagged edges that only fit one partner; glue seals the join.
low.analogy: Zipper tape cut so its teeth only mesh with one matching strand.
low.examPointer: Picture restriction enzymes as scissors and ligase as glue — the pairing image earns the explanation.

medium.restatement: Restriction enzymes cut DNA at sequence-specific sites, generating sticky ends of single-stranded DNA; the plasmid cut with the same enzyme offers complementary overhangs that anneal, and DNA ligase covalently joins the fragments into one unbroken recombinant molecule.
medium.analogy: A lock and key cut from the same blank — only one key fits one lock.
medium.examPointer: Always tie the same-enzyme rule to complementary sticky ends; that causal link is the mark.

check.stem: What do restriction enzymes do to DNA?

options.text: Cut it at specific base sequences
options.explanation: Correct — this follows directly from the definition.
Ligase does the joining.
That is transcription.
Replication enzymes do that.

check.stem: Why do different restriction enzymes cut DNA in different places?

options.text: Each type targets its own particular base sequence
options.explanation: Yes — the mechanism works exactly this way.

options.text: They cut randomly wherever they land
options.explanation: The cuts are sequence-specific.

options.text: They follow the shape of the cell
options.explanation: Cell shape plays no role.

options.text: They cut only at chromosome tips
options.explanation: Target sequences sit anywhere in DNA.

options.text: Their unpaired bases pair with complementary single-stranded overhangs
options.explanation: Correct — this matches the account taught above.

options.text: A glue coating applied in the lab
options.explanation: No physical glue exists on DNA.
Charge is not the pairing mechanism.
Pairing is chemical, not gripping.

check.stem: Which enzyme seals the gene into the opened plasmid?

options.explanation: Right — this is the account the lesson teaches.
Restriction enzymes cut; they do not seal.
Amylase works on starch.
Protease digests proteins.

check.stem: A gene and a plasmid show matching sticky ends. What follows?

options.text: They anneal and ligase joins them into one unbroken molecule
options.explanation: Right — the other options each misplace a concept.
Complementary ends attract by base pairing.
Cutting precedes the pairing stage.
The construct stays and functions.

check.stem: State the two enzyme types used to cut and join DNA.
check.modelAnswer: Restriction enzymes cut DNA at specific sites and DNA ligase joins the pieces together.

check.stem: Name the short single-stranded sections formed by cutting DNA.
check.modelAnswer: Cutting DNA with restriction enzymes leaves sticky ends that pair with complementary overhangs.

check.stem: Explain why the same restriction enzyme must cut both the gene and the plasmid.
check.modelAnswer: One enzyme leaves one overhang pattern, so both cut pieces end with complementary sticky ends that can base-pair, allowing ligase to complete the recombinant join.

check.stem: Designers want a gene inserted at one exact spot in a plasmid. Apply the sequence rule to explain the choice.
check.modelAnswer: Pick the restriction enzyme whose target sequence occurs once at that spot, so its cut opens the plasmid there and its sticky ends receive the gene precisely.

lessons.title: Vectors That Deliver the Cargo
lessons.opening: Recombinant DNA needs a courier. Plasmids ferry genes into bacteria and yeast, viruses deliver into human cells or bacteria, and once inside a bacterial host the plasmid rides cell division, spreading the gene through the growing population in a fermenter.
keyPoints: Plasmids and viruses act as vectors that take up DNA pieces and insert recombinant DNA into other cells.
Viruses deliver DNA into human cells or into bacteria.
Plasmids transfer DNA into bacteria or yeast.
Bacteria carrying the recombinant plasmid copy it at every division, spreading the gene as they multiply.
Engineered bacteria reproduce quickly inside a fermenter, and controlled conditions let the vessel yield large protein quantities.

low.restatement: A delivery van (plasmid or virus) carries the new gene into a cell; bacteria then photocopy the gene every time they divide.
low.analogy: A courier service with two vehicle types: vans for business parks (bacteria and yeast), motorbikes for city flats (human cells).
low.examPointer: Match vector to destination — viruses reach human cells or bacteria, plasmids reach bacteria or yeast.

medium.restatement: Vectors are plasmids or viruses that accept DNA fragments and deliver recombinant DNA into recipient cells, with viruses serving human cells or bacteria and plasmids serving bacteria or yeast; inside multiplying bacteria the plasmid is copied at each division, and fermenter growth yields large protein quantities.
medium.analogy: Postal workers with fixed delivery zones: each vector class delivers only to its assigned addresses.
medium.examPointer: Use the word vector explicitly, then name both vector types with their destinations for full credit.

check.stem: What is a vector in genetic engineering?

options.text: A plasmid or virus that carries DNA into other cells
options.explanation: Correct — this follows directly from the definition.
Enzymes cut and join; vectors carry.
Sequencing machines are not vectors.

options.text: A protein that reads the code
options.explanation: Reading proteins are not vectors.

check.stem: Which cells do viruses transfer DNA into?

options.explanation: Yes — the mechanism works exactly this way.
Yeast is the plasmid destination.
Plants are not the taught virus target here.
Spores are not the cited recipient.

check.stem: Which recipients accept DNA from plasmid vectors?

options.explanation: Correct — this matches the account taught above.
Human cells take viral delivery.
Muscle is not a plasmid target here.
Viruses are vectors, not recipients.

check.stem: How does a recombinant plasmid spread through a bacterial population?

options.text: The plasmid is copied whenever the bacteria reproduce
options.explanation: Right — this is the account the lesson teaches.

options.text: Plasmids migrate between cells like viruses
options.explanation: Copying at division does the spreading.

options.text: The gene mutates into new cells
options.explanation: No mutation is involved.
Natural reproduction handles distribution.

check.stem: A pharmaceutical team needs kilograms of a human protein. Complete the plan with the final stage.

options.text: Grow the engineered bacteria in fermenters under controlled conditions
options.explanation: Right — the other options each misplace a concept.

options.text: Inject the plasmids into patients directly
options.explanation: Patients receive purified protein, not plasmids.
Storage halts production, not scales it.
Crops play no role in this route.

check.stem: State the two structures that act as vectors for recombinant DNA.
check.modelAnswer: Plasmids and viruses act as vectors, taking up DNA and inserting it into other cells.

check.stem: Name the term for DNA assembled from separate source pieces.
check.modelAnswer: DNA combined from different pieces is called recombinant DNA.

check.stem: Explain why bacteria multiply so usefully for gene product manufacture.
check.modelAnswer: Bacterial division copies the recombinant plasmid into each descendant, so the population and its gene output grow exponentially in the fermenter.

check.stem: A therapy must reach human cells, not bacteria. Choose the vector and justify it.
check.modelAnswer: Choose a viral vector, because viruses transfer DNA into human cells, whereas plasmids serve bacteria or yeast.

glossary.definition: An enzyme that cuts DNA at particular base sequences.
A plasmid or virus that carries DNA into another cell.
DNA combined from pieces of different origin molecules.
A circular DNA molecule in bacteria used as a gene carrier.
